              f"isolated(-oo)={model.isolated(NEG_INF)}  -> {verdict}")
    survivors = [m.name for m in MODELS
                 if not (m.isolated(POS_INF) or m.isolated(NEG_INF))]
    print(f"\n  survivors: {survivors}")
    print("  matching the theorem: exactly two such topologies exist, the end")
    print("  compactification and its flip.")

    rule("4. THE DIVISION BOUNDARY")
    print("\n  (a) self-division x |-> x/x  (value PHI at 0, fin(1) elsewhere)")
    for model in MODELS:
        ok = self_division_discontinuous(model)
        print(f"      {model.name:>8}: discontinuous at 0 = {ok}   "
              f"(topology-canonical: true in every T1 model)")

    print("\n  (b) reciprocal y |-> 1/y, repaired at the origin")
    for model in MODELS:
        lim_r, lim_l = reciprocal_side_limits(model, thresholds)
        v = repairing_value(model, thresholds)
        print(f"      {model.name:>8}: lim_{{y->0+}} = {lim_r}, lim_{{y->0-}} = {lim_l}")
        if v is None:
            print("                unrepairable: the one-sided limits disagree, and a")
            print("                Hausdorff space has unique limits.")
        else:
            print(f"                repairable, uniquely, by v = {v}: the two ends are")
            print("                merged, so both sides share one limit.")

    rule("5. NUMERICAL WITNESS: 1/y approaching the origin")
    print("\n     y            1/y           natural       flip          circle")
    print("     " + "-" * 62)
    for k in (1, 3, 6, 9):
        for sign in (+1.0, -1.0):
            y = sign / (10.0 ** k)
            r = 1.0 / y
            cells: list[str] = []
            for model in MODELS:
                seq = [1.0 / (sign / (10.0 ** j)) for j in range(k, k + 25)]
                cells.append(str(limit_of_sequence(model, seq, thresholds)))
            print(f"   {y: .0e}   {r: .0e}     "
                  f"{cells[0]:<13} {cells[1]:<13} {cells[2]:<13}")

    print("\n  In the natural topology the two columns of one-sided limits differ")
    print("  (+oo against -oo), so no repair exists; in the flip they differ too,")
    print("  with the labels exchanged; in the circle model both sides give -oo,")
    print("  the single glue point, and that value repairs the reciprocal.\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: End Classification of a Finite Remainder by Neighbourhood Probing
algorithms.description: Given a compactification of the real line presented only by membership oracles for the basic neighbourhoods of its remainder points, this algorithm decides for each remainder point whether it is isolated, absorbs only the positive ray, absorbs only the negative ray, or absorbs both (a merged end), and then names the resulting model. Its correctness rests on the ends lemma: in a compact Hausdorff model in which the line sits openly, a remainder point that is a limit of finite values automatically meets finite values of arbitrarily large modulus, because the image of any closed bounded interval is compact and hence closed and can be deleted from a neighbourhood without destroying it. Therefore probing a single far point per threshold suffices, and the algorithm runs in O(T) oracle queries for T thresholds, with no search. By the uniqueness and classification theorems the resulting signature determines the topology: (positive, negative) is the end compactification, (negative, positive) is its flip, and a merged or isolated remainder point marks an exotic model.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT   member(a, b, p): is the point p in the basic neighbourhood N_b(a)?
        isolated(a):    is {a} open?
        thresholds:     an increasing finite list of real thresholds
OUTPUT  a signature for each exceptional point, and the name of the model

function ABSORBS_RAY(a, sign):
    if isolated(a): return false
    for each b in thresholds:
        x <- sign * (|b| + b + 1)          # a point strictly beyond b
        if not member(a, b, fin(x)): return false
    return true

function CLASSIFY(a):
    if isolated(a):                    return 'isolated'
    pos <- ABSORBS_RAY(a, +1)
    neg <- ABSORBS_RAY(a, -1)
    if pos and neg:                    return 'merged end'
    if pos:                            return 'positive end'
    if neg:                            return 'negative end'
    return 'limit point, not an end'

function IDENTIFY():
    sig <- { a |-> CLASSIFY(a) : a in {+oo, -oo, PHI} }
    if sig[+oo] = 'positive end' and sig[-oo] = 'negative end':
        return sig, 'end compactification (natural topology)'
    if sig[+oo] = 'negative end' and sig[-oo] = 'positive end':
        return sig, 'flip of the end compactification'
    if 'merged end' in values(sig):
        return sig, 'exotic: the two ends are identified (circle model)'
    return sig, 'not a two-ended compactification'

algorithms.name: Compact Core Radius and Ray Assignment for a Hausdorff Separation
algorithms.description: The computational shadow of the ray-separation lemma, the heart of the ends argument. Given disjoint open sets U around the first infinity and V around the second, the part of the space they fail to cover is closed in a compact space, hence compact, and contains no exceptional point, hence is a bounded set of reals. The algorithm searches an increasing grid for the least radius M beyond which both rays are fully covered by U union V, then reports which separator receives the positive ray and which the negative one, and finally verifies that the assignment does not oscillate along a ray. That last check is the discrete trace of connectedness: a connected ray covered by two disjoint open sets must lie entirely in one of them. When the two rays are assigned to different separators the model has two honest ends; when they are assigned to the same one, as in the circle model, the other remainder point cannot be an end and must be isolated. Cost: O(|grid| * |probes|) oracle queries, with a further O(S) for the constancy check over S samples.

algorithms.name: Continuity Test for a Repaired Reciprocal at the Origin
algorithms.description: Decides whether the reciprocal, given an arbitrary value at the origin, can be made continuous there in a presented model, and returns the unique repairing value when it exists. The method computes the limit of the finite values 1/y along y approaching zero from the right and from the left, entirely inside the model's own neighbourhood structure: a candidate remainder point is accepted as the limit when every basic neighbourhood of it contains the whole tail of the sample. A repair exists exactly when the two one-sided limits coincide, and then the repairing value is that common limit; uniqueness follows from Hausdorffness, since two repairs would give two limits along the punctured neighbourhood filter of the origin. The test returns 'no repair' for the end compactification and its flip — reproducing the ends-canonical sharpness theorem — and returns the glued infinity for the circle model, reproducing the unique-repair theorem. Cost: O(T * K) oracle queries for T thresholds and K samples; no search is needed, because the ends argument has already reduced the topology at the remainder to tail data.
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm C: Continuity test for a repaired reciprocal at the origin.

Given a compactification presented by neighbourhood bases, decide whether the
map

        rec_v(y) = v            if y = 0
                 = fin(1 / y)   otherwise

can be made continuous at the origin, and return the unique repairing value if
so. The test computes the limits of fin(1/y) along y -> 0+ and y -> 0- inside
the model's own neighbourhood structure: the repair exists exactly when the two
one-sided limits coincide, and then the repairing value is that common limit,
uniqueness following from Hausdorffness.

Complexity: O(T * K) membership queries for T thresholds and K sample points;
no search is required, because the ends argument has already reduced the
topology at the remainder to tail data.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Optional, Sequence

Point = tuple[str, float]
MembershipOracle = Callable[[str, float, Point], bool]
IsolationOracle = Callable[[str], bool]


def tail_limit(member: MembershipOracle, isolated: IsolationOracle,
               values: Sequence[float], thresholds: Sequence[float]) -> Optional[str]:
    """The exceptional point whose every basic neighbourhood contains the tail."""
    for a in ("+oo", "-oo", "PHI"):
        if isolated(a):
            continue
        tail = values[len(values) // 2:]
        if all(member(a, b, ("fin", x)) for b in thresholds for x in tail):
            return a
    return None


def one_sided_limits(member: MembershipOracle, isolated: IsolationOracle,
                     thresholds: Sequence[float], depth: int = 40
                     ) -> tuple[Optional[str], Optional[str]]:
    """Limits of fin(1/y) as y -> 0+ and as y -> 0-."""
    right = [10.0 ** k for k in range(1, depth)]     # 1/y for y = 10^-k
    left = [-(10.0 ** k) for k in range(1, depth)]   # 1/y for y = -10^-k
    return (tail_limit(member, isolated, right, thresholds),
            tail_limit(member, isolated, left, thresholds))


def repairing_value(member: MembershipOracle, isolated: IsolationOracle,
                    thresholds: Sequence[float]) -> Optional[str]:
    """The unique value repairing the reciprocal at the origin, or None."""
    right, left = one_sided_limits(member, isolated, thresholds)
    return right if (right is not None and right == left) else None


def verdict(member: MembershipOracle, isolated: IsolationOracle,
            thresholds: Sequence[float]) -> str:
    v = repairing_value(member, isolated, thresholds)
    if v is None:
        return ("no repair: the one-sided limits differ, so no value at the "
                "origin makes the reciprocal continuous (the guard is necessary)")
    return (f"repairable, uniquely, by v = {v}: the two ends are identified, "
            f"so both sides share a single limit (the guard is dispensable)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ths = [0.0, 1.0, 1e3, 1e9]

    def natural(a: str, b: float, p: Point) -> bool:
        if p[0] != "fin":
            return p[0] == a
        return p[1] > b if a == "+oo" else (p[1] < -b if a == "-oo" else False)

    def circle(a: str, b: float, p: Point) -> bool:
        if p[0] != "fin":
            return p[0] == a
        return abs(p[1]) > b if a == "-oo" else False

    print("natural:", verdict(natural, lambda a: a == "PHI", ths))
    print("circle :", verdict(circle, lambda a: a in ("PHI", "+oo"), ths))

visualizations.name: The Three Compact Models of the Transreal Carrier, Side by Side
visualizations.description: Draws the end compactification, its flip, and the circle model in one figure. The first two panels squash the whole real line into a closed interval with two distinct endpoints and shade the tail-ray neighbourhoods of each endpoint, with nullity as a detached square; the two panels differ only in the labels attached to the endpoints, making visible why the flip is a genuinely different topology on a named carrier while being the same space. The third panel draws the circle obtained by gluing the two ends into a single remainder point, with arrows showing both directions of escape arriving at the same place and with the isolated symbols drawn off to the sides. The figure explains at a glance why the reciprocal extends continuously across the circle but not across the interval.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation: the three compactifications of the real line side by side.

Left panel  : the end compactification, the line squashed into a closed
              interval with distinct endpoints -oo and +oo, plus an isolated
              nullity point. Basic neighbourhoods of the endpoints are tail
              rays, drawn as shaded caps.
Middle panel: its flip, identical as a space but with the two endpoint labels
              exchanged, so that x -> +infinity converges to the point named
              -oo.
Right panel : the circle model, in which the two ends are glued into a single
              remainder point, with +oo and nullity as isolated dots.

The picture makes visible why the reciprocal can be repaired on the circle and
not on the interval: on the circle the two escaping directions arrive at the
same place.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def squash(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """A homeomorphism R -> (-1, 1) used to draw the whole line in a finite box."""
    return x / (1.0 + np.abs(x))


def draw_interval(ax: plt.Axes, left_label: str, right_label: str, title: str,
                  b: float = 2.0) -> None:
    xs = np.linspace(-200.0, 200.0, 4001)
    ts = squash(xs)
    ax.plot(ts, np.zeros_like(ts), lw=3, color="#2b5c8a", solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.plot([-1.0], [0.0], "o", ms=11, color="#c0392b")
    ax.plot([1.0], [0.0], "o", ms=11, color="#c0392b")
    ax.text(-1.0, 0.16, left_label, ha="center", fontsize=13, color="#c0392b")
    ax.text(1.0, 0.16, right_label, ha="center", fontsize=13, color="#c0392b")
    tb = squash(np.array([b]))[0]
    ax.axvspan(tb, 1.02, color="#f0c419", alpha=0.35)
    ax.axvspan(-1.02, -tb, color="#7fb069", alpha=0.35)
    ax.text(0.0, -0.28, "tail-ray neighbourhoods of the two endpoints",
            ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#444")
    ax.plot([0.0], [0.62], "s", ms=10, color="#8e44ad")
    ax.text(0.0, 0.74, r"$\Phi$ (isolated)", ha="center", fontsize=11, color="#8e44ad")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlim(-1.25, 1.25)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.0)
    ax.axis("off")


def draw_circle(ax: plt.Axes, title: str, b: float = 2.0) -> None:
    theta = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 800)
    ax.plot(np.cos(theta) * 0.62, np.sin(theta) * 0.62 + 0.1, lw=3, color="#2b5c8a")
    ax.plot([0.0], [0.72], "o", ms=11, color="#c0392b")
    ax.text(0.0, 0.86, r"$-\infty$ (both ends glued)", ha="center",
            fontsize=11, color="#c0392b")
    cap = np.linspace(np.pi / 2 - 0.9, np.pi / 2 + 0.9, 200)
    ax.plot(np.cos(cap) * 0.62, np.sin(cap) * 0.62 + 0.1, lw=9,
            color="#f0c419", alpha=0.55, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.annotate("", xy=(0.13, 0.66), xytext=(0.55, 0.30),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#333"))
    ax.annotate("", xy=(-0.13, 0.66), xytext=(-0.55, 0.30),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#333"))
    ax.text(0.62, 0.22, r"$x\to+\infty$", fontsize=10)
    ax.text(-0.98, 0.22, r"$x\to-\infty$", fontsize=10)
    ax.plot([0.95], [0.1], "^", ms=11, color="#16a085")
    ax.text(0.95, -0.06, r"$+\infty$" + "\n(isolated)", ha="center", fontsize=10,
            color="#16a085")
    ax.plot([-0.95], [0.1], "s", ms=10, color="#8e44ad")
    ax.text(-0.95, -0.06, r"$\Phi$" + "\n(isolated)", ha="center", fontsize=10,
            color="#8e44ad")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlim(-1.3, 1.3)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.0)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")


def main() -> None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15.0, 4.4))
    draw_interval(axes[0], r"$-\infty$", r"$+\infty$",
                  "End compactification (natural topology)")
    draw_interval(axes[1], r"$+\infty$", r"$-\infty$",
                  "Flip: same space, exchanged labels")
    draw_circle(axes[2], "Circle model: the two ends merged")
    fig.suptitle("The three compact Hausdorff models of the transreal carrier",
                 fontsize=14)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("transreal_models.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote transreal_models.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: One-Sided Limits of the Reciprocal Inside Each Compactification
visualizations.description: Plots the reciprocal near the origin after mapping the target into a finite window, so that the remainder points become visible boundaries. In the upper panel, the natural topology, the right branch rises to the endpoint named plus infinity and the left branch falls to the endpoint named minus infinity, so the two one-sided limits are distinct points and no value at the origin can repair the map. In the lower panel, the circle model, both branches converge to the single glued point (drawn with the left branch lifted so the identification is explicit), and the reciprocal extends continuously across the origin. The two panels together are a picture of the dichotomy between topology-canonical and ends-canonical sharpness.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation: the reciprocal at the origin, seen inside each model.

The map y |-> 1/y is plotted after squashing the target into a finite box, so
that the two infinities become the top and bottom edges (interval models) or a
single shared edge (circle model).

Top row:    natural topology. The right branch climbs to the endpoint +oo, the
            left branch descends to the endpoint -oo: the two one-sided limits
            are different points, so no value at 0 makes the map continuous.
Bottom row: circle model. Both branches arrive at the same glued point, and
            assigning that value at the origin makes the reciprocal continuous
            on the whole line, uniquely.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def squash(v: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Homeomorphism R -> (-1, 1) rendering the endpoints of the interval model."""
    return v / (1.0 + np.abs(v))


def circle_angle(v: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Position on the circle model: both infinities map to the same point."""
    return 2.0 * np.arctan(v) / np.pi   # in (-1, 1), with +-1 identified


def main() -> None:
    ys_r = np.linspace(0.004, 1.0, 2000)
    ys_l = -ys_r[::-1]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9.0, 8.0), sharex=True)

    ax = axes[0]
    ax.plot(ys_r, squash(1.0 / ys_r), lw=2.2, color="#c0392b", label=r"$y>0$")
    ax.plot(ys_l, squash(1.0 / ys_l), lw=2.2, color="#2b5c8a", label=r"$y<0$")
    ax.axhline(1.0, ls="--", color="#c0392b", lw=1.2)
    ax.axhline(-1.0, ls="--", color="#2b5c8a", lw=1.2)
    ax.text(0.72, 0.93, r"endpoint $+\infty$", color="#c0392b", fontsize=11)
    ax.text(0.72, -0.99, r"endpoint $-\infty$", color="#2b5c8a", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("Natural topology: the one-sided limits are different endpoints\n"
                 "no value at the origin repairs the reciprocal", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_ylabel("position in the compactified target")
    ax.set_ylim(-1.15, 1.15)
    ax.legend(loc="center right")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

    ax = axes[1]
    ax.plot(ys_r, circle_angle(1.0 / ys_r), lw=2.2, color="#c0392b", label=r"$y>0$")
    ax.plot(ys_l, circle_angle(1.0 / ys_l) + 2.0, lw=2.2, color="#2b5c8a",
            label=r"$y<0$ (lifted: $-1 \sim +1$)")
    ax.axhline(1.0, ls="--", color="#16a085", lw=1.6)
    ax.text(0.6, 1.03, "the single glued point: both branches arrive here",
            color="#16a085", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("Circle model: the two ends are identified\n"
                 "the reciprocal extends continuously, with the glued point at 0",
                 fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$y$")
    ax.set_ylabel("position on the circle")
    ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 1.35)
    ax.legend(loc="center right")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("transreal_reciprocal.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote transreal_reciprocal.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.description: An interactive canvas that renders the end compactification, its flip, and the circle model simultaneously, with a draggable point x on the real line and an adjustable neighbourhood threshold b. As x moves the widget shows exactly where it sits in each model and reports which basic neighbourhood of which remainder point currently contains it, so the reader can feel the difference between an endpoint that absorbs the positive ray, one that absorbs the negative ray, a merged endpoint that absorbs both, and an isolated symbol that absorbs neither. Raising the threshold shrinks the shaded tail neighbourhoods and exposes the bounded compact core that the ends argument extracts from any Hausdorff separation of the two infinities; a running commentary explains, for the current position, whether the point is inside that core, committed to the positive ray, or committed to the negative ray, and why connectedness forbids a ray from being split between two disjoint open sets.

The Ends Explorer

The real line has exactly two ends: remove any bounded chunk [−M, M] and precisely two connected pieces remain, the rays (M, ∞) and (−∞, −M). A compactification with a two-point remainder must attach one point to each end — unless it cheats. Drag the point x along the line and watch where it travels in three compact Hausdorff models of the four-symbol carrier ℝ ∪ {+∞, −∞, Φ}. Raise the threshold b to shrink the basic neighbourhoods of the remainder points and see which ones still capture the moving point.

Natural topology

+∞ positive end −∞ negative end Basic neighbourhoods are tail rays: {+∞} ∪ (b, ∞) and {−∞} ∪ (−∞, −b). This is the extended real line, with nullity as an isolated dot.

Flip

+∞ negative end −∞ positive end The very same space with the two labels exchanged. It satisfies every axiom, has no isolated infinity, and is still a different topology on a carrier whose symbols are already named.

Circle

+∞ isolated −∞ merged end The two ends are glued into one point, named −∞; the symbol +∞ becomes a lonely dot that nothing approaches. Compact, Hausdorff, line open inside, nullity isolated — and not the natural topology.

interactive_layout:
# How Many Ways Can You Cap Off the Number Line? *A guided tour of the uniqueness and classification of two-point transreal compactifications.* --- ## 0. The problem in one picture Total arithmetic wants to give a value to every expression, including $1/0$. The standard way is to enlarge the real line with three symbols, $$\mathbb{T} \;=\; \{\,\mathrm{fin}(x) : x \in \mathbb{R}\,\}\;\cup\;\{+\infty\}\;\cup\;\{-\infty\}\;\cup\;\{\Phi\},$$ and legislate $1/0 = +\infty$, $(-1)/0 = -\infty$, $0/0 = \Phi$ ("nullity"). Nothing crashes. But to say whether an operation is *continuous* you must say which points of $\mathbb{T}$ are near which — you must choose a **topology**. The usual choice is the extended real line $[-\infty,+\infty]$ with $\Phi$ as an isolated dot. **The question of this page:** is that choice forced, or is it a convention we made and then forgot we had made? Spoiler: it is *almost* forced. Four natural axioms leave exactly two survivors once one pathological model is excluded, and a single extra condition — an *orientation* — pins it down completely. And the pathological model turns out to be the one place in the universe where dividing by zero is continuous. --- ## 1. Meet the three models Before any proofs, get the geometry into your hands. Drag the point $x$ along the line and see where it travels in each candidate topology. Raise the threshold $b$ to shrink the neighbourhoods of the infinities and watch which ones still catch the moving point. {{interactive_demo:0}} Three things to notice while you play: * In the **natural topology**, pushing $x$ to the right sends it to $+\infty$ and pushing it left sends it to $-\infty$. The two remainder points sit at opposite endpoints of an interval. * In the **flip topology**, the picture is identical but the *labels* are swapped. As a space it is the same interval; as a topology on a carrier whose four symbols already have names, it is genuinely different. * In the **circle model**, the two directions of escape arrive at the *same* point, and the symbol $+\infty$ becomes a lonely dot that no sequence of finite numbers ever approaches.
Why is a “lonely dot” allowed? (the four axioms, stated precisely) Call a topology $\tau$ on $\mathbb{T}$ a **transreal compactification** when 1. **(C)** $(\mathbb{T},\tau)$ is compact — nothing escapes; 2. **(H)** $(\mathbb{T},\tau)$ is Hausdorff — distinct points have disjoint neighbourhoods, so limits are unique; 3. **(L)** $\mathrm{fin}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{T}$ is an open embedding — the finite arithmetic is topologically untouched; 4. **(N)** $\{\Phi\}$ is open — nullity is an error value, never a limit. The circle model satisfies all four: a circle together with two isolated dots is compact and Hausdorff, the circle minus its glue point is a copy of $\mathbb{R}$ sitting openly inside, and $\Phi$ is isolated. Nothing in the list says that $+\infty$ must be near anything. That is the loophole.
--- ## 2. The real line has exactly two ends Here is the classical idea that makes everything work. Delete a bounded chunk $[-M,M]$ from $\mathbb{R}$; two connected pieces remain, the rays $(M,\infty)$ and $(-\infty,-M)$. Enlarge the chunk and you still get two pieces, nested inside the previous ones. Those two nested families are the **ends** of the line: the two essentially different ways to leave every bounded region. Read more about [ends of a space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_(topology)) and about [compactification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compactification_(mathematics)) if the notion is new. A compactification with a finite remainder is nothing more than a decision about how to attach points to ends. Two remainder points, two ends: either you attach one to each (the interval), or you attach one point to both and leave the other spare (the circle). The following algorithm turns that intuition into a decision procedure. It takes a model presented only by *neighbourhood bases at the remainder points* and reports, for each exceptional symbol, whether it is isolated, the positive end, the negative end, or a merged end — and thereby names the model. {{algorithm:0}} --- ## 3. The engine: how the ends force the topology Suppose you are handed a mystery topology satisfying the four axioms, plus the orientation conditions $$+\infty \in \overline{\{\mathrm{fin}(x) : x>0\}}, \qquad -\infty \in \overline{\{\mathrm{fin}(x): x<0\}}.$$ The claim is that the mystery topology is *exactly* the natural one. The proof has four movements, and each is worth seeing on its own.
Movement 1 — an infinity glued to a ray absorbs the whole ray Let $W$ be any open set containing $+\infty$, and let $c$ be any bound. Put $d=|c|$. The set $\mathrm{fin}([-d,d])$ is the continuous image of a compact interval, hence compact, hence **closed** because the space is Hausdorff. So $$W' = W \setminus \mathrm{fin}([-d,d])$$ is still open, and still contains $+\infty$ (no exceptional point is a finite point). Since $+\infty$ lies in the closure of the positive finite points, $W'$ must meet them: there is $x>0$ with $\mathrm{fin}(x) \in W'$, and being outside $[-d,d]$ forces $x > d \ge c$. Conclusion: every neighbourhood of $+\infty$ contains *arbitrarily large* positive numbers. The infinity is a genuine end, not merely a limit point.
Movement 2 — a compact core bounds everything that is not yet separated Hausdorffness gives disjoint open $U_0 \ni +\infty$ and $V_0 \ni -\infty$. Nullity is both open and closed, so we may replace them by $U_1 = U_0 \cup \{\Phi\}$ and $V_1 = V_0 \setminus \{\Phi\}$ — still open, still disjoint, and now every point they miss is finite. What they miss is closed inside a compact space, hence compact; pulled back along the embedding it is a compact, therefore **bounded**, set of reals. So there is a radius $M$ beyond which the whole line is swallowed by $U_1 \cup V_1$.
Movement 3 — connectedness makes each ray commit, and the ends split them The ray $(M,\infty)$ is connected, so its image is connected, so it cannot be broken between two disjoint open sets: it lies wholly in $U_1$ or wholly in $V_1$. Same for $(-\infty,-M)$. Could both rays choose $U_1$? Then $V_1$ — an open neighbourhood of $-\infty$ — would contain no finite point of large modulus at all, contradicting Movement 1. So the rays split, one to each infinity. Which one goes where is precisely what the orientation hypothesis decides; without it, both splits are possible, and *that* is the flip ambiguity.
Movement 4 — forced neighbourhoods, then a collision of topologies Combining the previous movements: for every $b$, the set $U_1 \setminus \mathrm{fin}([-R,R])$ with $R = \max(M,|b|)$ is an open neighbourhood of $+\infty$ contained in $\{+\infty\} \cup \mathrm{fin}((b,\infty))$. But those tail sets are exactly the basic neighbourhoods of $+\infty$ in the extended real line. So at each of the four kinds of point — finite points by the open-embedding axiom, $\Phi$ by isolation, the two infinities by the tail rays — every natural-topology open set contains a mystery-topology neighbourhood. Hence **every natural-open set is mystery-open**. The last step is free and is one of the small miracles of general topology: *a compact topology finer than a Hausdorff topology equals it.* The identity map runs continuously from the compact side to the Hausdorff side; a continuous map from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is closed; so the inverse is continuous too. The two topologies coincide.
The second movement is the one with genuine computational content. This algorithm computes the core radius $M$ from a presented separation and reports which separator receives which ray — and verifies numerically that the assignment never oscillates, which is the discrete trace of connectedness. {{algorithm:1}} > **Uniqueness Theorem.** A topology on the four-symbol carrier equals the natural topology $[-\infty,+\infty] \sqcup \{\Phi\}$ **if and only if** it is compact and Hausdorff, contains the finite line as an open copy of $\mathbb{R}$, isolates nullity, and orients its two infinities as the positive and negative ends of the line. --- ## 4. What the hypotheses are worth Every hypothesis above earns its place, and the two exotic models show why. * Drop the orientation entirely and the **circle model** slips through: all four axioms, and yet $+\infty$ is isolated. * Try to patch this by demanding *density* — that no exceptional point other than $\Phi$ be isolated — and the **flip model** slips through: no isolated infinity, both infinities honest ends, and still not the natural topology. What survives is a complete census. > **Classification Theorem.** If a compact Hausdorff topology on the carrier contains the line openly, isolates nullity, and isolates neither infinity, then it is the natural topology or its flip — and nothing else. In classical language: *a two-point-remainder compactification of the two-ended, locally compact real line, in which both remainder points are limit points, is the end compactification* — the only residual freedom being which end is labelled $+\infty$. {{visualization:0}} --- ## 5. Now the payoff: can you divide by zero? Here is where the abstraction earns its keep. Two "sharpness" facts justify the guards in transreal arithmetic, and they turn out to have *different logical status*. Play with the laboratory below: pick a model, then squeeze $y$ towards zero from both sides and watch the two one-sided tracks of $1/y$. {{interactive_demo:1}} **Self-division.** The map $x \mapsto x/x$ equals $1$ everywhere except at the origin, where the arithmetic returns $\Phi$. In *any* topology in which points are closed — the mildest separation axiom there is — this is discontinuous at $0$, because every punctured neighbourhood value is $1$ and $1 \ne \Phi$. No compactification, however clever, smooths it out. Call such a statement **topology-canonical**. **The reciprocal.** In the natural topology no value at the origin makes $y \mapsto 1/y$ continuous: the right-hand limit is $+\infty$, the left-hand limit is $-\infty$, and a Hausdorff space forbids two limits. The same holds in the flip model — compose with the label-swapping involution and the failure transports. By the classification, therefore, it holds in *every* model whose infinities are honest ends. Call such a statement **ends-canonical**. But in the circle model the reciprocal **is** continuous, once you set $1/0$ to the glued point, and that value is the only one that works. So the necessity of the guard on division is a fact about *the shape of the remainder*, not about the four-symbol carrier. {{algorithm:2}} {{visualization:1}} | statement | status | |---|---| | $x \mapsto x/x$ is discontinuous | **topology-canonical** — every $T_1$ model | | no value repairs $y \mapsto 1/y$ at $0$ | **ends-canonical** — exactly the two-ended models; fails on the circle | --- ## 6. Run the whole story yourself The following self-contained program reproduces every claim on this page numerically: it recovers the end signature of each model, computes the compact core radius and the ray assignment, checks that exactly two models survive the classification hypotheses, and decides repairability of the reciprocal in each. {{demo:0}}
What exactly is being computed here? Each model is encoded not as a set of open sets — an uncountable object — but as a **membership oracle** for basic neighbourhoods: $$N_b(+\infty) = \{+\infty\} \cup \mathrm{fin}((b,\infty)), \qquad N_b(-\infty) = \{-\infty\} \cup \mathrm{fin}((-\infty,-b)),$$ with the circle model replacing the second by $N_b(-\infty) = \{-\infty\} \cup \mathrm{fin}(\{|x|>b\})$ and declaring $\{+\infty\}$ open. This is legitimate precisely *because* of the theorem: the ends argument shows the topology at the remainder is nothing but tail data, so probing tails is probing the topology. Everything then reduces to finitely many membership queries.
--- ## 7. Where this goes next * **An ends functor.** Only three facts about $\mathbb{R}$ were used: local compactness, that the complement of a compact core has exactly two components, and that those components are connected. Replace "two rays" by "the components of the complements of a compact exhaustion" and the argument should give: finite-remainder compactifications of a locally compact space with finitely many ends are exactly the quotients of its end compactification. * **Does the algebra see the topology?** The flip ambiguity is invisible to topology but *not* to arithmetic: $1 \cdot (+\infty) = +\infty$ while $1 \cdot (-\infty) = -\infty$, and the label swap does not commute with multiplication by positive scalars. So the orientation topology cannot supply may be forced by requiring multiplication to be continuous — which would make the transreal line rigid outright. * **Guard necessity as an invariant of the remainder.** The circle model repairs $1/y$ exactly because its remainder is a quotient of the end space. The general conjecture: an unbounded continuous function extends across a compactification if and only if the remainder separates its limit behaviour along the ends. If you take one thing away, let it be this: **whether you can divide by zero depends on whether you kept the two ends of the number line apart.**

import Cryptography.Transreal.Topology

/-!
# The transreal carrier as an end compactification: a uniqueness theorem

`Cryptography.Transreal.Topology` topologises the four-constructor carrier

```
Transreal ::= fin ℝ | pinf | ninf | null
```

*by fiat*, as the two-point compactification `EReal` of the line disjointly
unioned with an isolated point for nullity.  The purpose of this file is to show
that this choice is **forced**, and to locate exactly the hypothesis that forces
it.

## The structure of the argument

Write `t` for an arbitrary topology on the carrier.  We call `t` a
*transreal compactification* (`Transreal.IsCompactification`) when

* `t` is compact Hausdorff;
* `fin : ℝ → Transreal` is a `t`-open embedding;
* `{null}` is `t`-open.

These are exactly the axioms of the informal conjecture.  They do **not**
suffice (see `Novelty.TransrealExoticTopology`): the complement of `{null}` is a
compact Hausdorff space containing `ℝ` as an open subspace with a two-point
remainder, but such a space need not be the *end* compactification — one of the
two remainder points may be an isolated point sitting beside a **circle**
(the one-point compactification of the line).

What rules the exotic models out is an *orientation*, i.e. the requirement that
each infinity really is an end of the line:

```
hp : pinf ∈ closure (fin '' Ioi 0)      hn : ninf ∈ closure (fin '' Iio 0)
```

The main theorem `Transreal.topology_eq_of_isCompactification` says that these
two conditions upgrade the axioms to a **complete characterisation**:

```
t = Transreal.instTopologicalSpace ↔ IsCompactification t ∧ hp ∧ hn
```

so every sharpness statement proved in the natural topology is
topology-canonical relative to the ends data, not an artefact of the model.

## The ends argument

The engine is a genuine ends argument for the real line:

* `Transreal.exists_gt_mem_of_isOpen` / `Transreal.exists_lt_mem_of_isOpen`:
  every `t`-neighbourhood of `pinf` (resp. `ninf`) contains **arbitrarily large
  positive** (resp. **arbitrarily large negative**) finite points.  This is the
  statement that the infinities are ends and not merely limit points.
* `Transreal.exists_rays`: separating the two infinities produces a compact
  `t`-closed core inside the finite fragment, hence a radius `M` outside which
  the line is covered by the two separating open sets; connectedness of the
  rays `Ioi M`, `Iio (-M)` forces each ray into a single one of them, and the
  ends property forces the two rays into *different* ones.
* `Transreal.exists_nhd_pinf` / `Transreal.exists_nhd_ninf`: consequently the
  sets `{pinf} ∪ fin '' (Ioi b)` and `{ninf} ∪ fin '' (Iio b)` are
  neighbourhood bases at the two infinities — which is precisely the
  neighbourhood filter of `⊤` and `⊥` in `EReal`.
* Finally a compact-to-Hausdorff comparison upgrades the resulting inequality
  of topologies to equality.
-/

namespace Transreal

open Set Topology Filter

/-! ### The axioms of a transreal compactification -/

/-- A topology `t` on the four-constructor carrier is a *transreal
compactification* when it is compact Hausdorff, makes the finite fragment an
open copy of the line, and isolates nullity.  These are the axioms of the
uniqueness conjecture. -/
structure IsCompactification (t : TopologicalSpace Transreal) : Prop where
  /-- The carrier is `t`-compact. -/
  compactSpace : @CompactSpace Transreal t
  /-- The carrier is `t`-Hausdorff. -/
  t2Space : @T2Space Transreal t
  /-- The finite fragment is an open copy of the line. -/
  isOpenEmbedding_fin : @IsOpenEmbedding ℝ Transreal _ t fin
  /-- Nullity is isolated. -/
  isOpen_null : IsOpen[t] ({null} : Set Transreal)


theorem pinf_ne_ninf : (pinf : Transreal) ≠ ninf := fun h => Transreal.noConfusion h

theorem pinf_notMem_range_fin : (pinf : Transreal) ∉ range fin := by
  rintro ⟨x, hx⟩; cases hx

theorem ninf_notMem_range_fin : (ninf : Transreal) ∉ range fin := by
  rintro ⟨x, hx⟩; cases hx

theorem null_notMem_range_fin : (null : Transreal) ∉ range fin := by
  rintro ⟨x, hx⟩; cases hx


/-! ### The natural topology: it satisfies the axioms, and its neighbourhood filters

Everything in this section is about the *fixed* natural topology
`Transreal.instTopologicalSpace`; no variable topology is in scope. -/

theorem isOpenEmbedding_toSum : IsOpenEmbedding toSum :=
  ⟨isEmbedding_toSum, by rw [toSum_surjective.range_eq]; exact isOpen_univ⟩

theorem tendsto_fin_atTop : Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => fin x) atTop (𝓝 pinf) := by
  rw [isEmbedding_toSum.tendsto_nhds_iff]
  have h1 : Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => ((x : EReal))) atTop (𝓝 (⊤ : EReal)) :=
    EReal.tendsto_coe_nhds_top_iff.2 tendsto_id
  exact (continuous_inl.tendsto _).comp h1

theorem tendsto_fin_atBot : Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => fin x) atBot (𝓝 ninf) := by
  rw [isEmbedding_toSum.tendsto_nhds_iff]
  have h1 : Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => ((x : EReal))) atBot (𝓝 (⊥ : EReal)) :=
    EReal.tendsto_coe_nhds_bot_iff.2 tendsto_id
  exact (continuous_inl.tendsto _).comp h1

/-- In the natural topology `pinf` is a limit of positive finite values: it is the
positive end of the line. -/
theorem pinf_mem_closure : pinf ∈ closure (fin '' Ioi (0 : ℝ)) := by
  refine mem_closure_of_tendsto tendsto_fin_atTop ?_
  filter_upwards [eventually_gt_atTop (0 : ℝ)] with x hx
  exact ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩

/-- In the natural topology `ninf` is a limit of negative finite values: it is the
negative end of the line. -/
theorem ninf_mem_closure : ninf ∈ closure (fin '' Iio (0 : ℝ)) := by
  refine mem_closure_of_tendsto tendsto_fin_atBot ?_
  filter_upwards [eventually_lt_atBot (0 : ℝ)] with x hx
  exact ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩

/-- The natural topology is a transreal compactification in the sense of
`Transreal.IsCompactification`. -/
theorem isCompactification_instTopologicalSpace :
    IsCompactification instTopologicalSpace where
  compactSpace := instCompactSpace
  t2Space := instT2Space
  isOpenEmbedding_fin := isOpenEmbedding_fin
  isOpen_null := isOpen_singleton_null

/-- A natural-topology neighbourhood of `pinf` contains a whole tail ray: the
neighbourhood filter of `pinf` is that of `⊤ : EReal`. -/
theorem exists_ray_subset_of_isOpen_pinf {s : Set Transreal} (hs : IsOpen s)
    (ha : pinf ∈ s) : ∃ b : ℝ, insert pinf (fin '' Ioi b) ⊆ s := by
  obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ : ∃ b : ℝ, Ioi (b : EReal) ⊆ Sum.inl ⁻¹' (toSum '' s) :=
    EReal.mem_nhds_top_iff.1
      (IsOpen.mem_nhds ((isOpenEmbedding_toSum.isOpenMap _ hs).preimage continuous_inl)
        ⟨pinf, ha, rfl⟩)
  refine ⟨b, ?_⟩
  rintro a (rfl | ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩)
  · exact ha
  · have hx' : ((x : ℝ) : EReal) ∈ Ioi (b : EReal) := Set.mem_Ioi.2 (EReal.coe_lt_coe_iff.2 hx)
    obtain ⟨y, hy, hy'⟩ := hb hx'
    have hyx : y = fin x := toSum_injective hy'
    rwa [hyx] at hy

/-- A natural-topology neighbourhood of `ninf` contains a whole tail ray: the
neighbourhood filter of `ninf` is that of `⊥ : EReal`. -/
theorem exists_ray_subset_of_isOpen_ninf {s : Set Transreal} (hs : IsOpen s)
    (ha : ninf ∈ s) : ∃ b : ℝ, insert ninf (fin '' Iio b) ⊆ s := by
  obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ : ∃ b : ℝ, Iio (b : EReal) ⊆ Sum.inl ⁻¹' (toSum '' s) :=
    EReal.mem_nhds_bot_iff.1
      (IsOpen.mem_nhds ((isOpenEmbedding_toSum.isOpenMap _ hs).preimage continuous_inl)
        ⟨ninf, ha, rfl⟩)
  refine ⟨b, ?_⟩
  rintro a (rfl | ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩)
  · exact ha
  · have hx' : ((x : ℝ) : EReal) ∈ Iio (b : EReal) := Set.mem_Iio.2 (EReal.coe_lt_coe_iff.2 hx)
    obtain ⟨y, hy, hy'⟩ := hb hx'
    have hyx : y = fin x := toSum_injective hy'
    rwa [hyx] at hy

/-- A natural-topology neighbourhood of a finite point contains the image of an
open set of reals. -/
theorem isOpen_preimage_fin_of_isOpen {s : Set Transreal} (hs : IsOpen s) :
    IsOpen (fin ⁻¹' s) := hs.preimage continuous_fin

/-- In the natural topology, `pinf` is **not** isolated. -/
theorem not_isOpen_singleton_pinf : ¬ IsOpen ({pinf} : Set Transreal) := by
  intro hopen
  obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := exists_ray_subset_of_isOpen_pinf hopen rfl
  have : fin (b + 1) ∈ ({pinf} : Set Transreal) := hb (Or.inr ⟨b + 1, by simp, rfl⟩)
  simp at this

/-- In the natural topology, `ninf` is **not** isolated. -/
theorem not_isOpen_singleton_ninf : ¬ IsOpen ({ninf} : Set Transreal) := by
  intro hopen
  obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := exists_ray_subset_of_isOpen_ninf hopen rfl
  have : fin (b - 1) ∈ ({ninf} : Set Transreal) := hb (Or.inr ⟨b - 1, by simp, rfl⟩)
  simp at this


section Ends

variable {t : TopologicalSpace Transreal}

/-! ### The two infinities are ends -/

/-- **The positive end.**  If `pinf` is a limit of positive finite values then
every `t`-neighbourhood of `pinf` contains arbitrarily large positive finite
values.  (The upgrade from "some" to "arbitrarily large" uses only that compact
subsets of the line are `t`-closed.) -/
theorem exists_gt_mem_of_isOpen (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hp : pinf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Ioi 0))
    {W : Set Transreal} (hW : IsOpen[t] W) (hpW : pinf ∈ W) (c : ℝ) :
    ∃ x : ℝ, c < x ∧ fin x ∈ W := by
  letI := t
  haveI := h.t2Space
  have hcont : Continuous (fin : ℝ → Transreal) := h.isOpenEmbedding_fin.continuous
  set d : ℝ := |c| with hd
  have hd0 : 0 ≤ d := abs_nonneg c
  have hL : IsClosed (fin '' Icc (-d) d) := (isCompact_Icc.image hcont).isClosed
  have hW' : IsOpen (W \ fin '' Icc (-d) d) := hW.sdiff hL
  have hpW' : pinf ∈ W \ fin '' Icc (-d) d := by
    refine ⟨hpW, ?_⟩
    rintro ⟨x, -, hx⟩
    cases hx
  obtain ⟨y, hy1, hy2⟩ := mem_closure_iff.1 hp _ hW' hpW'
  obtain ⟨x, hx0, rfl⟩ := hy2
  refine ⟨x, ?_, hy1.1⟩
  have hxnot : x ∉ Icc (-d) d := fun hx => hy1.2 ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
  have hx0' : (0 : ℝ) < x := hx0
  have : d < x := by
    by_contra hcon
    exact hxnot ⟨by linarith, by linarith⟩
  calc c ≤ |c| := le_abs_self c
    _ = d := hd.symm
    _ < x := this

/-- **The negative end.**  The mirror image of `Transreal.exists_gt_mem_of_isOpen`. -/
theorem exists_lt_mem_of_isOpen (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hn : ninf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Iio 0))
    {W : Set Transreal} (hW : IsOpen[t] W) (hnW : ninf ∈ W) (c : ℝ) :
    ∃ x : ℝ, x < c ∧ fin x ∈ W := by
  letI := t
  haveI := h.t2Space
  have hcont : Continuous (fin : ℝ → Transreal) := h.isOpenEmbedding_fin.continuous
  set d : ℝ := |c| with hd
  have hd0 : 0 ≤ d := abs_nonneg c
  have hL : IsClosed (fin '' Icc (-d) d) := (isCompact_Icc.image hcont).isClosed
  have hW' : IsOpen (W \ fin '' Icc (-d) d) := hW.sdiff hL
  have hnW' : ninf ∈ W \ fin '' Icc (-d) d := by
    refine ⟨hnW, ?_⟩
    rintro ⟨x, -, hx⟩
    cases hx
  obtain ⟨y, hy1, hy2⟩ := mem_closure_iff.1 hn _ hW' hnW'
  obtain ⟨x, hx0, rfl⟩ := hy2
  refine ⟨x, ?_, hy1.1⟩
  have hxnot : x ∉ Icc (-d) d := fun hx => hy1.2 ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
  have hx0' : x < (0 : ℝ) := hx0
  have : x < -d := by
    by_contra hcon
    exact hxnot ⟨by linarith, by linarith⟩
  have : -d ≤ c := by
    have := neg_abs_le c
    linarith [hd ▸ this]
  linarith

/-! ### The ray partition -/

/-- **The two-point remainder splits the two rays.**  Assume only that each
infinity is *unoriented end data*: every neighbourhood of it contains finite
points of arbitrarily large modulus.  Then there is a radius `M` and a pair of
disjoint open sets, one containing `pinf`, the other `ninf`, neither containing
nullity, such that the two rays `(M, ∞)` and `(-∞, -M)` are separated by them —
in one order or the other.

This is the ends argument proper: a compact `t`-closed core inside the finite
fragment bounds the part of the line that is not yet separated, connectedness of
each ray sends it wholly into one of the two open sets, and the end property
forbids the two rays from choosing the same one. -/
theorem exists_rays_aux (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hfarP : ∀ W : Set Transreal, IsOpen[t] W → pinf ∈ W → ∀ c : ℝ,
      ∃ x : ℝ, c < |x| ∧ fin x ∈ W)
    (hfarN : ∀ W : Set Transreal, IsOpen[t] W → ninf ∈ W → ∀ c : ℝ,
      ∃ x : ℝ, c < |x| ∧ fin x ∈ W) :
    ∃ (M : ℝ) (U V : Set Transreal), IsOpen[t] U ∧ IsOpen[t] V ∧
      pinf ∈ U ∧ ninf ∈ V ∧ Disjoint U V ∧ null ∉ U ∧ null ∉ V ∧
      (((∀ x : ℝ, M < x → fin x ∈ U) ∧ (∀ x : ℝ, x < -M → fin x ∈ V)) ∨
        ((∀ x : ℝ, M < x → fin x ∈ V) ∧ (∀ x : ℝ, x < -M → fin x ∈ U))) := by
  letI := t
  haveI := h.t2Space
  haveI := h.compactSpace
  have hcont : Continuous (fin : ℝ → Transreal) := h.isOpenEmbedding_fin.continuous
  obtain ⟨U0, V0, hU0, hV0, hpU0, hnV0, hUV0⟩ := t2_separation (pinf_ne_ninf)
  -- Enlarge `U0` by nullity so that the uncovered core lies inside the line.
  set U1 : Set Transreal := U0 ∪ {null} with hU1def
  set V1 : Set Transreal := V0 \ {null} with hV1def
  have hnullclosed : IsClosed ({null} : Set Transreal) := isClosed_singleton
  have hU1 : IsOpen U1 := hU0.union h.isOpen_null
  have hV1 : IsOpen V1 := hV0.sdiff hnullclosed
  have hdisj : Disjoint U1 V1 := by
    rw [Set.disjoint_left]
    rintro a (haU | ha) haV
    · exact (Set.disjoint_left.1 hUV0 haU) haV.1
    · exact haV.2 ha
  -- The core is compact and lies inside the finite fragment.
  have hKclosed : IsClosed ((U1 ∪ V1)ᶜ) := (hU1.union hV1).isClosed_compl
  have hKcompact : IsCompact ((U1 ∪ V1)ᶜ) := hKclosed.isCompact
  have hKsub : (U1 ∪ V1)ᶜ ⊆ range fin := by
    intro a ha
    cases a with
    | fin x => exact ⟨x, rfl⟩
    | pinf => exact absurd (Or.inl (Or.inl hpU0)) ha
    | ninf => exact absurd (Or.inr ⟨hnV0, by simp⟩) ha
    | null => exact absurd (Or.inl (Or.inr rfl)) ha
  have himg : fin '' (fin ⁻¹' ((U1 ∪ V1)ᶜ)) = (U1 ∪ V1)ᶜ :=
    Set.image_preimage_eq_of_subset hKsub
  have hS : IsCompact (fin ⁻¹' ((U1 ∪ V1)ᶜ)) := by
    rw [h.isOpenEmbedding_fin.isEmbedding.isCompact_iff, himg]
    exact hKcompact
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ : ∃ M : ℝ, ∀ x ∈ fin ⁻¹' ((U1 ∪ V1)ᶜ), |x| ≤ M := by
    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hS.bddAbove
    obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := hS.bddBelow
    refine ⟨max a (-b), fun x hx => abs_le.2 ⟨?_, ?_⟩⟩
    · have h1 : b ≤ x := hb hx
      have h2 : -b ≤ max a (-b) := le_max_right _ _
      linarith
    · exact le_trans (ha hx) (le_max_left _ _)
  have hcover : ∀ x : ℝ, M < |x| → fin x ∈ U1 ∪ V1 := by
    intro x hx
    by_contra hcon
    exact absurd (hM x hcon) (not_le.2 hx)
  -- Each ray is connected, hence lands entirely in one of the two open sets.
  have hopenU : IsOpen (fin ⁻¹' U1) := hU1.preimage hcont
  have hopenV : IsOpen (fin ⁻¹' V1) := hV1.preimage hcont
  have hdisjpre : Disjoint (fin ⁻¹' U1) (fin ⁻¹' V1) := by
    rw [Set.disjoint_left]
    intro x hx hx'
    exact (Set.disjoint_left.1 hdisj hx) hx'
  have hIoi : Ioi M ⊆ fin ⁻¹' U1 ∨ Ioi M ⊆ fin ⁻¹' V1 := by
    refine IsPreconnected.subset_or_subset hopenU hopenV hdisjpre ?_ isPreconnected_Ioi
    intro x hx
    have hx' : M < |x| := lt_of_lt_of_le hx (le_abs_self x)
    exact hcover x hx'
  have hIio : Iio (-M) ⊆ fin ⁻¹' U1 ∨ Iio (-M) ⊆ fin ⁻¹' V1 := by
    refine IsPreconnected.subset_or_subset hopenU hopenV hdisjpre ?_ isPreconnected_Iio
    intro x hx
    have hx' : M < |x| := by
      have : x < -M := hx
      have : M < -x := by linarith
      calc M < -x := this
        _ ≤ |x| := neg_le_abs x
    exact hcover x hx'
  -- The end property forbids both rays from choosing the same side.
  have hnotUU : ¬ (Ioi M ⊆ fin ⁻¹' U1 ∧ Iio (-M) ⊆ fin ⁻¹' U1) := by
    rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
    obtain ⟨x, hx, hxV⟩ := hfarN V1 hV1 ⟨hnV0, by simp⟩ M
    rcases lt_abs.1 hx with hpos | hneg
    · exact (Set.disjoint_left.1 hdisj (h1 hpos)) hxV
    · exact (Set.disjoint_left.1 hdisj (h2 (by simp only [Set.mem_Iio]; linarith))) hxV
  have hnotVV : ¬ (Ioi M ⊆ fin ⁻¹' V1 ∧ Iio (-M) ⊆ fin ⁻¹' V1) := by
    rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
    obtain ⟨x, hx, hxU⟩ := hfarP U1 hU1 (Or.inl hpU0) M
    rcases lt_abs.1 hx with hpos | hneg
    · exact (Set.disjoint_left.1 hdisj hxU) (h1 hpos)
    · exact (Set.disjoint_left.1 hdisj hxU) (h2 (by simp only [Set.mem_Iio]; linarith))
  have hcase : ((Ioi M ⊆ fin ⁻¹' U1) ∧ (Iio (-M) ⊆ fin ⁻¹' V1)) ∨
      ((Ioi M ⊆ fin ⁻¹' V1) ∧ (Iio (-M) ⊆ fin ⁻¹' U1)) := by
    rcases hIoi with h1 | h1 <;> rcases hIio with h2 | h2
    · exact absurd ⟨h1, h2⟩ hnotUU
    · exact Or.inl ⟨h1, h2⟩
    · exact Or.inr ⟨h1, h2⟩
    · exact absurd ⟨h1, h2⟩ hnotVV
  refine ⟨M, U1 \ {null}, V1, hU1.sdiff hnullclosed, hV1, ⟨Or.inl hpU0, by simp⟩,
    ⟨hnV0, by simp⟩, Disjoint.mono_left Set.diff_subset hdisj, by simp,
    fun hc => hc.2 rfl, ?_⟩
  rcases hcase with ⟨h1, h2⟩ | ⟨h1, h2⟩
  · exact Or.inl ⟨fun x hx => ⟨h1 hx, by simp⟩, fun x hx => h2 hx⟩
  · exact Or.inr ⟨fun x hx => h1 hx, fun x hx => ⟨h2 hx, by simp⟩⟩

/-- Every neighbourhood of `pinf` contains finite points of arbitrarily large
modulus, given the positive orientation. -/
theorem far_of_pinf_mem_closure (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hp : pinf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Ioi 0)) :
    ∀ W : Set Transreal, IsOpen[t] W → pinf ∈ W → ∀ c : ℝ, ∃ x : ℝ, c < |x| ∧ fin x ∈ W := by
  intro W hW hpW c
  obtain ⟨x, hx, hxW⟩ := exists_gt_mem_of_isOpen h hp hW hpW |c|
  refine ⟨x, ?_, hxW⟩
  have h1 : x ≤ |x| := le_abs_self x
  have h2 : c ≤ |c| := le_abs_self c
  linarith

/-- Every neighbourhood of `ninf` contains finite points of arbitrarily large
modulus, given the negative orientation. -/
theorem far_of_ninf_mem_closure (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hn : ninf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Iio 0)) :
    ∀ W : Set Transreal, IsOpen[t] W → ninf ∈ W → ∀ c : ℝ, ∃ x : ℝ, c < |x| ∧ fin x ∈ W := by
  intro W hW hnW c
  obtain ⟨x, hx, hxW⟩ := exists_lt_mem_of_isOpen h hn hW hnW (-|c|)
  refine ⟨x, ?_, hxW⟩
  have h1 : -x ≤ |x| := neg_le_abs x
  have h2 : c ≤ |c| := le_abs_self c
  linarith

/-- **The ends separate the two rays.**  Under the compactification axioms
together with the two orientation conditions, the ray `(M, ∞)` lands in a
neighbourhood of `pinf` and the ray `(-∞, -M)` in a disjoint neighbourhood of
`ninf`. -/
theorem exists_rays (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hp : pinf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Ioi 0))
    (hn : ninf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Iio 0)) :
    ∃ (M : ℝ) (U V : Set Transreal), IsOpen[t] U ∧ IsOpen[t] V ∧
      pinf ∈ U ∧ ninf ∈ V ∧ Disjoint U V ∧ null ∉ U ∧ null ∉ V ∧
      (∀ x : ℝ, M < x → fin x ∈ U) ∧ (∀ x : ℝ, x < -M → fin x ∈ V) := by
  obtain ⟨M, U, V, hU, hV, hpU, hnV, hUV, hnullU, hnullV, hcase⟩ :=
    exists_rays_aux h (far_of_pinf_mem_closure h hp) (far_of_ninf_mem_closure h hn)
  rcases hcase with ⟨h1, h2⟩ | ⟨h1, h2⟩
  · exact ⟨M, U, V, hU, hV, hpU, hnV, hUV, hnullU, hnullV, h1, h2⟩
  · exfalso
    obtain ⟨x, hx, hxU⟩ := exists_gt_mem_of_isOpen h hp hU hpU M
    exact (Set.disjoint_left.1 hUV hxU) (h1 x hx)

/-! ### Neighbourhood bases at the two infinities -/

/-- The sets `{pinf} ∪ fin '' (Ioi b)` are a neighbourhood basis at `pinf`:
this is exactly the neighbourhood filter of `⊤` in `EReal`. -/
theorem exists_nhd_pinf (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hp : pinf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Ioi 0))
    (hn : ninf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Iio 0)) (b : ℝ) :
    ∃ W : Set Transreal, IsOpen[t] W ∧ pinf ∈ W ∧ W ⊆ insert pinf (fin '' Ioi b) := by
  letI := t
  haveI := h.t2Space
  have hcont : Continuous (fin : ℝ → Transreal) := h.isOpenEmbedding_fin.continuous
  obtain ⟨M, U, V, hU, hV, hpU, hnV, hUV, hnullU, hnullV, hrayU, hrayV⟩ :=
    exists_rays h hp hn
  set d : ℝ := max b M with hd
  have hdb : b ≤ d := le_max_left _ _
  have hdM : M ≤ d := le_max_right _ _
  have hL : IsClosed (fin '' Icc (-d) d) := (isCompact_Icc.image hcont).isClosed
  refine ⟨U \ fin '' Icc (-d) d, hU.sdiff hL, ⟨hpU, by rintro ⟨x, -, hx⟩; cases hx⟩, ?_⟩
  rintro a ⟨haU, haL⟩
  cases a with
  | fin x =>
      have hxnot : x ∉ Icc (-d) d := fun hx => haL ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
      rcases not_and_or.1 hxnot with hlow | hhigh
      · exfalso
        have hx : x < -M := by
          have : ¬ (-d ≤ x) := hlow
          push_neg at this
          linarith
        exact (Set.disjoint_left.1 hUV haU) (hrayV x hx)
      · have hx : d < x := by push_neg at hhigh; exact hhigh
        exact Or.inr ⟨x, lt_of_le_of_lt hdb hx, rfl⟩
  | pinf => exact Or.inl rfl
  | ninf => exact absurd haU (Set.disjoint_left.1 hUV.symm hnV)
  | null => exact absurd haU hnullU

/-- The sets `{ninf} ∪ fin '' (Iio b)` are a neighbourhood basis at `ninf`:
this is exactly the neighbourhood filter of `⊥` in `EReal`. -/
theorem exists_nhd_ninf (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hp : pinf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Ioi 0))
    (hn : ninf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Iio 0)) (b : ℝ) :
    ∃ W : Set Transreal, IsOpen[t] W ∧ ninf ∈ W ∧ W ⊆ insert ninf (fin '' Iio b) := by
  letI := t
  haveI := h.t2Space
  have hcont : Continuous (fin : ℝ → Transreal) := h.isOpenEmbedding_fin.continuous
  obtain ⟨M, U, V, hU, hV, hpU, hnV, hUV, hnullU, hnullV, hrayU, hrayV⟩ :=
    exists_rays h hp hn
  set d : ℝ := max (-b) M with hd
  have hdb : -b ≤ d := le_max_left _ _
  have hdM : M ≤ d := le_max_right _ _
  have hL : IsClosed (fin '' Icc (-d) d) := (isCompact_Icc.image hcont).isClosed
  refine ⟨V \ fin '' Icc (-d) d, hV.sdiff hL, ⟨hnV, by rintro ⟨x, -, hx⟩; cases hx⟩, ?_⟩
  rintro a ⟨haV, haL⟩
  cases a with
  | fin x =>
      have hxnot : x ∉ Icc (-d) d := fun hx => haL ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
      rcases not_and_or.1 hxnot with hlow | hhigh
      · have hx : x < -d := by push_neg at hlow; exact hlow
        refine Or.inr ⟨x, ?_, rfl⟩
        have : -d ≤ b := by linarith
        exact lt_of_lt_of_le hx this
      · exfalso
        have hx : M < x := by
          push_neg at hhigh
          linarith
        exact (Set.disjoint_left.1 hUV (hrayU x hx)) haV
  | pinf => exact absurd haV (Set.disjoint_left.1 hUV hpU)
  | ninf => exact Or.inl rfl
  | null => exact absurd haV hnullV


/-! ### The uniqueness theorem -/

/-- Every natural-topology open set is `t`-open.  This is the comparison half of
the uniqueness theorem: it is proved by exhibiting, at each of the four kinds of
point, a `t`-neighbourhood inside the given natural-topology open set — the
finite points by the open-embedding axiom, nullity by the isolation axiom, and
the two infinities by the ray bases `exists_nhd_pinf`, `exists_nhd_ninf`
produced by the ends argument. -/
theorem le_of_isCompactification (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hp : pinf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Ioi 0))
    (hn : ninf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Iio 0)) :
    t ≤ instTopologicalSpace := by
  letI := t
  have hcts : @Continuous Transreal Transreal t instTopologicalSpace id := by
    rw [continuous_def]
    intro s hs
    have hmain : ∀ a ∈ s, ∃ W : Set Transreal, IsOpen[t] W ∧ a ∈ W ∧ W ⊆ s := by
      intro a ha
      cases a with
      | fin x =>
          refine ⟨fin '' (fin ⁻¹' s), h.isOpenEmbedding_fin.isOpenMap _
            (isOpen_preimage_fin_of_isOpen hs), ⟨x, ha, rfl⟩, ?_⟩
          rintro _ ⟨y, hy, rfl⟩
          exact hy
      | null => exact ⟨{null}, h.isOpen_null, rfl, by rintro _ rfl; exact ha⟩
      | pinf =>
          obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := exists_ray_subset_of_isOpen_pinf hs ha
          obtain ⟨W, hW, hpW, hWsub⟩ := exists_nhd_pinf h hp hn b
          exact ⟨W, hW, hpW, hWsub.trans hb⟩
      | ninf =>
          obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := exists_ray_subset_of_isOpen_ninf hs ha
          obtain ⟨W, hW, hnW, hWsub⟩ := exists_nhd_ninf h hp hn b
          exact ⟨W, hW, hnW, hWsub.trans hb⟩
    have : IsOpen[t] s := by
      rw [isOpen_iff_mem_nhds]
      intro a ha
      obtain ⟨W, hW, haW, hWs⟩ := hmain a ha
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset (hW.mem_nhds haW) hWs
    simpa using this
  exact continuous_id_iff_le.1 hcts

/-- **Uniqueness of the two-point transreal compactification.**  A topology on
the four-constructor carrier is the natural one (`EReal ⊔ {Φ}`) as soon as it is
compact Hausdorff, makes the finite fragment an open copy of the line, isolates
nullity, and orients the two infinities as the two ends of the line.

The two orientation hypotheses are not removable: `Novelty.TransrealExoticTopology`
exhibits a compact Hausdorff topology satisfying all the other requirements yet
differing from the natural one. -/
theorem topology_eq_of_isCompactification (h : IsCompactification t)
    (hp : pinf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Ioi 0))
    (hn : ninf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Iio 0)) :
    t = instTopologicalSpace := by
  have hle : t ≤ instTopologicalSpace := le_of_isCompactification h hp hn
  refine le_antisymm hle ?_
  -- The reverse inequality: a compact topology finer than a Hausdorff one is equal
  -- to it, because the identity is then a closed map.
  have hcts : @Continuous Transreal Transreal t instTopologicalSpace id :=
    continuous_id_iff_le.2 hle
  rw [TopologicalSpace.le_def]
  intro s hs
  have hclosed : @IsClosed Transreal t sᶜ := @isClosed_compl_iff Transreal t s |>.2 hs
  have hcompact : @IsCompact Transreal t sᶜ :=
    @IsClosed.isCompact Transreal t sᶜ h.compactSpace hclosed
  have himg : @IsCompact Transreal instTopologicalSpace sᶜ := by
    have h2 := @IsCompact.image Transreal Transreal t instTopologicalSpace sᶜ id hcompact hcts
    simpa using h2
  have hcl : @IsClosed Transreal instTopologicalSpace sᶜ :=
    @IsCompact.isClosed Transreal instTopologicalSpace instT2Space sᶜ himg
  simpa using hcl.isOpen_compl

/-- The characterisation in biconditional form: the natural topology is *exactly*
the compact Hausdorff topology in which the line sits openly, nullity is isolated,
and the infinities are the two ends. -/
theorem topology_eq_iff :
    t = instTopologicalSpace ↔
      IsCompactification t ∧ pinf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Ioi 0) ∧
        ninf ∈ @closure Transreal t (fin '' Iio 0) := by
  constructor
  · rintro rfl
    exact ⟨isCompactification_instTopologicalSpace, pinf_mem_closure, ninf_mem_closure⟩
  · rintro ⟨h, hp, hn⟩
    exact topology_eq_of_isCompactification h hp hn

end Ends
